 Social Security COLA 3.6% vs 3.4% wage growth: will retirees gain more buying power than workers earning wages in 2027, and is inflation eating the raise?
 SECTIONS Social Security COLA 3.6% vs 3.4% wage growth: will retirees gain more buying power than workers earning wages in 2027, and is inflation eating the raise? By Piyush Shukla , Global Desk Last Updated: Oct 29, 2026, 11:11:00 PM IST Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment Synopsis Social Security benefits are set to increase by 3.6% in 2027, but will retirees actually feel richer? The answer depends on how quickly everyday expenses rise. Workers face a different test, as salary increases may fall behind inflation. For both groups, higher income will offer real relief only if it keeps pace with rising living costs.
 Social Security COLA rises 3.6% in 2027, but will retirees gain more buying power than workers earning wages? Social Security payments in the US will go up by 3.6% from January 2027. The Social Security Administration (SSA) has announced this Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) for about 72 million beneficiaries. It looks like a decent raise.
 What does the 3.6% Social Security COLA for 2027 actually mean?
A COLA is not a bonus. It is a yearly adjustment meant to help benefits keep pace with rising prices. The SSA checks consumer prices in the third quarter of the year and uses that to set the increase.
Take a simple example. If a retiree gets $2,000 a month today, a 3.6% rise adds $72, taking the payment to $2,072. Useful, but it only helps if prices have not already eaten that amount. 
And prices are still rising. The consumer price index went up 3.7% year over year in September, above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. The two numbers cover different periods, so they cannot be compared one to one, but the gap is small. Inflation has cooled since its 2022 peak, yet living costs still shape retirees’ budgets.
The COLA follows inflation both ways. In 2022, after prices jumped following the COVID-19 pandemic, the SSA announced an 8.7% COLA for 2023.
 Live Events
 The SSA has also shared an update on its records. It says it has corrected nearly 50 million Social Security number records since January 2025. This includes 17 million missing dates of death and about 25 million records with missing citizenship information. Another 8.5 million records with wrong citizenship details are still being fixed.
 Are retirees really ahead of workers who stay in their jobs?
On the latest numbers, yes, but only slightly. The three-month moving average of year-over-year median wage growth for job stayers, up to September, was 3.4%. That is below the 3.6% COLA .
 Wages work differently from the COLA. They depend on what employers can pay, how much demand there is for a worker’s skills, how the industry is doing, and whether the person changes jobs. A COLA depends only on prices.
Retirees have not always come out ahead. Over the past six years, they got a bigger increase than job stayers in three of those years. That is half the time. So the 0.2 percentage point lead this year is real, but it is not a pattern you can depend on.
 Should workers switch jobs in 2027 to earn more?
Recent figures show that people who changed employers saw faster pay growth than both job stayers and the 3.6% COLA. Individual results vary, though, and switching is not an easy route right now.
Hiring in the US has been slow. Layoffs are low, but job openings are limited. Some white-collar industries have lost jobs, and employment in leisure and hospitality has gone up and down.
This “low-hire, low-fire” market gives some safety to people who already have a job. But it can also weaken their position when they ask for a raise. Some employees are responding by making their work more visible to managers and to their professional networks.
What could happen next depends on prices. If inflation stays near the September level, the 3.6% raise will leave retirees roughly where they are now. If it falls, retirees will gain some real income. For workers, the pay gap between switching and staying will stay wide as long as hiring stays slow.
